title: German–Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty
subtitle: Turning conquest into a settlement
body:
Warsaw’s surrender on 28 September 1939 coincided with negotiations in Moscow intended to give the conquest of Poland a durable political form. Ribbentrop and Molotov’s Boundary and Friendship Treaty addressed the division of territory, but its accompanying agreements reached into trade, population movements and the suppression of Polish political activity. The settlement is best understood as an attempt to organise cooperation between occupiers whose military gains had not secured the acceptance of Poland or its allies. Its central problem was how to consolidate those gains while avoiding disputes between the powers that had made them. The coincidence mattered, but it could mislead. Warsaw’s capitulation was a military surrender, not a Polish signature on the partition of the republic. The treaty proceeded from the claim that Poland had ceased to exist and that Germany and the Soviet Union could therefore arrange its affairs between themselves. Polish representatives rejected that claim. Within days, they were explaining abroad that losing control of the national territory had not transferred the right to dispose of it to the invading powers. The dispute concerned the survival of a state as well as the fate of its land. [1] [2] The [August pact](/articles/molotov-ribbentrop-pact-1939-08-23) and the successive [German](/articles/german-invasion-poland-1939-09-01) and [Soviet](/articles/soviet-invasion-poland-1939-09-17) invasions created the conditions for these negotiations. September’s settlement then revised the earlier allocation of interests and sought to regulate the relationship emerging on the ground. This chapter follows the mechanisms of that consolidation: the definition of the boundary, the exchange concerning Lithuania, the treatment of political opposition and migration, and the economic commitments that accompanied the public appeal for peace. Warsaw’s capitulation did not end the campaign. Modlin held until **29 September**, the Hel Peninsula until **2 October**, and organised fighting continued around Kock until **6 October**. [3] These later dates matter to the meaning of the agreement: the governments in Moscow were claiming political finality while Polish troops still resisted. A capitulation could bind the forces surrendering at a particular place without authorising two foreign states to extinguish Poland. The treaty’s assertion of settlement consequently ran ahead of events on the battlefield as well as against the position maintained by Polish diplomacy. [4] [5]

Returning to Moscow with a different bargain

The secret protocol of 23 August had left some matters open. It envisaged a division of interests in Polish territory approximately along the Narew, Vistula and San, but reserved the question of whether an independent Polish state should survive. That reservation was disappearing by late September. In a telegram describing his meeting with Stalin and Molotov on 25 September, the German ambassador, Friedrich-Werner von der Schulenburg, reported Stalin’s opposition to leaving a Polish rump state. Stalin presented such a state as a potential cause of future disagreement between the two powers. This was a German diplomatic account of the conversation, but it recorded a specific proposal subsequently reflected in the settlement. [6] [7] Stalin offered Germany the Lublin province and the part of Warsaw province extending to the Bug, in exchange for relinquishing German claims to Lithuania. His intervention helps explain why the eventual boundary differed from the August arrangement. The revision was not simply the result of German troops having advanced farther than anticipated. Soviet leadership was actively bargaining over the shape of the occupation and the direction in which Soviet influence should expand. Berlin gained a larger share of central Poland; Moscow gained German acceptance of its predominant interest in Lithuania. The same conversation linked agreement over Poland to further Soviet action in the Baltic region. [7] Ribbentrop arrived in Moscow on the evening of 27 September. A timetable preserved among the papers of German diplomat Andor Hencke places the first meeting that night and further discussions on the following afternoon. Dinner at the Kremlin and an act of *Swan Lake* interrupted the schedule before talks resumed at midnight. The brief record places the signing at five in the morning, after that resumption. The documents nevertheless bear the date 28 September, which is the treaty’s historical and legal date. This small discrepancy between the calendar of the talks and the date written on the agreement is a reminder that diplomatic anniversaries often compress negotiations that continued through the night. [8]

What five public articles tried to settle

The public treaty was short enough to conceal its ambition behind administrative language. Article I identified the boundary of German and Soviet interests through an attached map, with further description to follow. Article II declared the line definitive and rejected intervention by other powers. Article III assigned administrative reorganisation west of the line to Germany and east of it to the Soviet Union. Article IV presented the settlement as a basis for friendship between their peoples. Article V required ratification but made the agreement effective upon signature. The preamble’s reference to the “former Polish state” was the political premise supporting the whole construction. [9] The treaty’s administrative language rested on an asserted authority that Poland had never conceded. The signatories undertook to reorganise territory acquired through invasion, without a Polish agreement or consultation of its inhabitants. Their demand for finality also addressed other governments: recognition of the new boundary would remove Poland’s territorial future from further negotiation. The signatures established a commitment between Germany and the Soviet Union, but acceptance of the political settlement remained an objective of their diplomacy. Potocki’s subsequent protest demonstrates that this objective was actively contested. [9] [2] The revised division placed much of the central stretch of the boundary on the Bug, farther east than the earlier Vistula division. A report sent from Berlin by the American chargé, Alexander Kirk, on 29 September described the published route from the vicinity of Lithuania through the northern river system, along the Bug and eventually to the San. It was a report of the German news agency’s description, rather than a field survey. Its value lies in showing what was being announced to the outside world: the partners had replaced a provisional arrangement with a declared territorial settlement, including a new allocation of land in central Poland. [10] Implementation required further decisions after the line had been declared definitive. Steinhardt’s dispatch of 5 October reported a supplementary protocol signed the previous day and a mixed commission to arrange frontier details; a later report recorded ratification on 19 October. These stages explain how a treaty effective on signature could still leave work for surveyors and administrators. Their actions would translate the diplomatic division into crossing arrangements and jurisdictions. The interval is important to the atlas because the treaty date alone cannot establish the position of every unit or the date on which every locality experienced the new boundary. [11] [12]

Reading the atlas

A partition line is not a battlefront

The 28 September map shows an approximate trace of the agreed partition. It should not be read as proof that all troops had reached their final positions that day. The later demarcation work also means that the treaty date and the physical marking of the frontier must be kept separate. A diplomatic map records what governments agreed to claim; an operational map must establish where forces actually were. [11]

Lithuania in the balance

The territorial revision had another side that remained secret. Lithuania was transferred into the Soviet sphere of influence, while Germany acquired the specified additional Polish territory. The supplementary protocol also preserved a prospective German claim to a strip in southwestern Lithuania and protected existing German–Lithuanian economic agreements. These details expose the transactional character of the bargain. Lithuania was neither a defeated participant in the Polish campaign nor a consenting party to this agreement. Its future was being discussed as something two larger neighbours could exchange for advantages elsewhere. [13] This was an allocation of influence, not the immediate annexation of Lithuania. That distinction mattered because coercion would proceed through further steps, with their own documents and public explanations. On 10 October, Lithuania concluded a mutual assistance treaty with the Soviet Union. In return for Vilnius and its surrounding district, the agreement permitted Soviet bases and garrisons on Lithuanian territory. Steinhardt’s report the following morning noted that their numbers and locations were to be settled separately. Moscow was able to attach a powerful inducement to a grave restriction of Lithuanian freedom of action: the recovery of a city Lithuania claimed, but which had been under Polish rule before the invasion. [14] The October agreement confronted Lithuania with an inducement inseparable from a strategic concession. Recovery of Vilnius satisfied a longstanding claim while Soviet military access restricted the government’s freedom of action. Poles in Wilno confronted another transfer arranged without Polish participation. The eventual Soviet occupation and incorporation of Lithuania occurred in 1940; they should remain distinct from the sphere allocated in September and the basing agreement of October. Following these successive instruments shows how diplomatic pressure could narrow a smaller state’s choices before the later destruction of its independence. [15] The southwestern strip remained a source of private manoeuvring. Ribbentrop’s instructions of 4 October, transmitted early on 5 October, recorded that Molotov had informed the Lithuanian foreign minister of the confidential arrangement. Berlin now had to explain its own claim. The instructions presented the proposed transfer as a practical correction to an awkward border, while reserving Germany’s right to decide when it should occur. Germany also wanted Soviet troops kept out of the strip. The episode shows how a settlement advertised as clear and final could still contain deferred claims, controlled disclosures and competing preferences over implementation. [16]

A smaller state’s predicament

The price attached to Vilnius

The October agreement offered Lithuania a long-sought city together with Soviet military installations. Those terms should be read together. The territorial gain helped make a coercive strategic arrangement presentable as a diplomatic success. Neither the transfer of Vilnius nor the secret allocation of Lithuania’s sphere represented Polish consent to the disposal of territory. [14]

Polish politics and populations behind the new line

Another secret protocol addressed the possibility that Poles might refuse to accept the settlement in practice. Each government undertook to suppress Polish agitation in its territory when that activity affected the other party’s territory, and to inform its partner about suitable measures. The clause was brief, but its political meaning was substantial. The occupiers understood that an imposed boundary would not necessarily divide Polish loyalties or the desire to restore independence. They promised cooperation against a form of activity that could connect opposition on both sides. [17] The agitation protocol identifies a specific undertaking whose evidentiary scope must be respected. It commits each occupier to suppress the designated activity affecting the other’s territory and to exchange information about measures taken. Establishing particular police conferences, operations or crimes requires additional records. The clause nevertheless reveals what the negotiators considered necessary for consolidation: an imposed frontier would not sever Polish political loyalties, so opposition capable of reaching across it required cooperation between the authorities on either side. [17] A confidential population protocol approached the inhabitants from a different direction. Moscow agreed not to obstruct the departure of German nationals and people of German descent who wished to move to Germany or German-administered territory. Transfers were to be conducted by German agents working with the local authorities, with emigrants’ property rights protected. Berlin assumed a corresponding obligation for people of Ukrainian or Belarusian descent in its area. The document’s language concerned people wishing to migrate. It was not a blanket authorisation for every forced displacement that followed. Yet its categories showed the occupiers organising movement according to ancestry across a frontier the affected population had not chosen. [18] The population agreement’s protections applied to specified categories of emigrants. It contained no equivalent general provision enabling Polish or Jewish communities to determine their political future, and its property assurances cannot be extended to every displaced household. This selectivity gave ancestry an administrative consequence: some movements could proceed through agents and official cooperation while other inhabitants confronted uncertain permission to cross. The protocol therefore belongs to the history of how the occupiers classified people, as well as to the history of migration itself. [18]

The resources and railways inside the bargain

The economic correspondence accompanying the treaty is easily overshadowed by its map. It deserves attention because the new relationship had to function during a continuing European war. In an exchange of letters dated 28 September, the Soviet government committed itself to developing a programme of raw-material deliveries, to be compensated by German manufactured goods over a longer period. The parties proposed restoring trade to the highest volume previously reached and beginning negotiations promptly. This was a framework for expanded exchange, rather than a complete list of deliveries already made. [19] The exchange linked German demand for resources under wartime economic pressure to Soviet demand for manufactured goods. Its different delivery schedules also introduced a continuing question of performance: raw materials might be supplied before complex industrial orders could be completed. The agreement thus created obligations extending beyond the diplomatic encounter, with each government dependent on subsequent negotiation and fulfilment. Economic cooperation was a process requiring transport, production and compensation; the existence of a signed programme supplies no evidence that all promised goods had already moved. [19] [20] The confidential letter made this economic geography unusually concrete. It promised facilitation of German transit towards Romania on the Upper Silesia–Lemberg–Kolomea railway and towards Iran, Afghanistan and the Far East. Its petroleum provision used the annual production of Drohobycz–Borysław to define an additional quantity, but specified that half would come from that district and half from other Soviet fields, in exchange for coal and steel piping. This detail qualifies the familiar association of partition with possession of resources: the arrangement combined a regional production benchmark with a wider Soviet supply obligation. It recorded a promise whose fulfilment still required deliveries. [21]

Poland refuses to disappear

The clearest Polish answer arrived in the language of diplomacy rather than a battlefield communiqué. On 30 September, Ambassador Jerzy Potocki informed the United States, on his government’s instructions, that the Moscow agreement violated existing treaties and international law. Poland refused to recognise it and intended to recover its occupied territory and its people’s freedom and self-determination. The note was short, direct and addressed to another government. Its significance lay partly in the ordinary diplomatic act itself: the representative of the allegedly extinguished state was continuing to speak and be received as its representative. [2] Institutional continuity depended on maintaining communication despite the internment of Poland’s senior authorities in Romania. The Polish foreign ministry’s historical account emphasises Ambassador Roger Raczyński’s role in contacts between the interned leadership and politicians in France, including the transfer of the presidency from Ignacy Mościcki to Władysław Raczkiewicz. These procedures preserved a basis for recognised government after the loss of effective territorial administration. They demonstrate that continuity was sustained through specific decisions and diplomatic work under severe constraint, rather than by the intact survival of offices inside occupied Poland. [22] On 30 September, Raczkiewicz became president in exile and General Władysław Sikorski became prime minister in France. The government’s initial base was France; its move to Britain followed France’s defeat in 1940. Keeping that sequence clear matters because the familiar phrase “London government” can obscure the immediate effort to reconstitute Polish authority in the autumn of 1939. The leaders now operating abroad were trying to preserve a state that had lost the ability to protect people at home. Their continued existence offered no immediate relief at a checkpoint, but it ensured that military defeat did not become an uncontested diplomatic surrender. [23] The United States gave an explicit answer of its own. A statement issued by Secretary of State Cordell Hull on 2 October affirmed that Washington continued to regard the Polish government as existing despite Poland’s subjection to force. The statement is recorded in an editorial note in the State Department’s documentary collection. Recognition was not military rescue, and the United States remained outside the European war. Nevertheless, this position contradicted the legal and political premise on which Berlin and Moscow had presented their settlement. The continued war against Germany and the survival of Polish diplomacy meant that the partition remained internationally disputed. [24]

London and Paris read the same treaty differently

The joint declaration issued with the treaty tried to turn the occupation of Poland into an argument for ending the European war. Germany and the Soviet Union announced that their settlement had created the basis for peace in eastern Europe, called for an end to the conflict between Germany and the Western powers, and assigned Britain and France responsibility if efforts to end it failed. They also promised consultation about further measures. The sequence of the argument was convenient for both signatories: their conquests were treated as settled before the opponents of those conquests were invited to make peace. [25] On 3 October, Neville Chamberlain described the agreement in the House of Commons as an attempted fourth partition of Poland. He identified the frontier settlement, the peace declaration and the projected economic relationship as connected developments. Britain, he argued, had entered the war against a recurring pattern of German aggression; Poland’s defeat had not removed that reason. His response rejected the suggestion that successful conquest entitled Germany to dictate when the international consequences of its attack should end. The speech also made clear that further promises from Hitler’s government would be judged against its record of broken undertakings. [26] The parliamentary discussion was less uniform than that central statement suggests. In the same debate, David Lloyd George urged a different treatment of the Soviet role, while Labour’s David Grenfell condemned the Soviet intervention and argued that the presence of two aggressors did not diminish the wrong done to Poland. The exchange illustrates a continuing difficulty for British politics: opposition to Germany did not produce a single view of Moscow. Arguments about Soviet security, former imperial frontiers and future strategic rivalry could coexist with recognition that the Soviet Union had participated in Poland’s destruction. [26] Private British assessments were cautious about predicting an unlimited alliance. Joseph Kennedy’s report of 30 September described Foreign Office officials as expecting Moscow to benefit from a prolonged conflict among the Western powers while remaining outside that war. They considered direct Soviet military commitment to Germany unlikely, though the warmth of Ribbentrop’s reception caused concern. The British ambassador in Moscow even raised the possible value of trade incentives in influencing Soviet conduct. These were judgments about interests and possible policy, not privileged knowledge of Stalin’s future decisions. They help explain how condemnation of the partition could coexist with efforts to avoid extending the war to the Soviet Union. [27] French anxiety also produced claims that exceeded the evidence available to diplomats. On 30 September, Alexis Léger told Bullitt that Moscow had promised Germany 2,000 bombers for an attack on France, a statement the American ambassador questioned. The dispatch is valuable as evidence of the threat perceived within the French foreign ministry. It does not establish a Soviet bomber commitment. Preserving Bullitt’s scepticism is essential, because the archival survival of an alarming report can otherwise lend authority to the very uncertainty it records. [28] French concern did not immediately produce a decision to break with Moscow. On 7 October, the French chargé there told Steinhardt that the developing partnership had caused him to reconsider his earlier opposition to a rupture. He was contemplating recommending a firmer policy, potentially including a break in relations, and asked how American representation of French interests might be arranged. He expressly described the inquiry as anticipatory. Preserving that qualification matters: a diplomat exploring a contingency was not announcing a decision by his government. [29] Publicly, Édouard Daladier insisted on security that would last. Chamberlain’s statement of 12 October, replying to Hitler’s subsequent peace proposals, cited the French premier’s broadcast two days earlier and stressed the need for dependable guarantees. Britain and France would not accept conquest as a sufficient foundation for peace merely because Germany now offered negotiations. Their position sustained the war against Germany, although it had not saved Poland from occupation. For Poles, that distinction was painfully concrete: continued allied belligerency preserved a future possibility of liberation while leaving the immediate balance of force inside their country unchanged. [30]

Selling the peace in Germany and the Soviet Union

The German government had a domestic audience for its peace initiative as well as a foreign one. Reports assembled by SOPADE, the German Social Democrats in exile, described hopes that the defeat of Poland would allow the war to end quickly. The reports also recorded reluctance toward a wider conflict and popular irritation with wartime restrictions. They came from opponents of the Nazi regime using incomplete underground reporting, so they cannot be treated as a representative opinion poll. They do, however, challenge the image of a German public uniformly eager for a prolonged European war. [31] Moscow’s public language moved decisively in support of the relationship. In his speech to the Supreme Soviet on 31 October, Molotov defended German–Soviet friendship and presented Germany as seeking peace while Britain and France pursued the war for imperial aims. Steinhardt’s report noted Molotov’s argument that a strong Germany was necessary for European peace, together with his favourable account of the ongoing economic negotiations. This was an official justification of policy, not evidence that ordinary Soviet citizens had reached the same conclusions. It showed the Soviet leadership lending its authority to the diplomatic argument Germany wanted the Western powers to accept. [32]

The boundary as people encountered it

For refugees, the settlement could turn a temporary flight into an indefinite separation. People who had moved east to escape the German advance now faced an emerging barrier across the country. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum records guarded crossings, arbitrary violence and the danger of travelling without papers. Some exhausted refugees returned towards German-held territory because home and family seemed preferable to remaining without money or a destination. These were decisions made under immediate pressure and incomplete knowledge, not informed choices between the later histories of two occupation systems. [33] The settlement made movement predictable for selected purposes while leaving many ordinary journeys exposed to arbitrary control. Its migration categories supported specified transfers, and its economic letters addressed commercial transit; neither created a general right for inhabitants to rejoin relatives across the frontier. The same railway could consequently form part of a negotiated supply route and remain inaccessible to a refugee. This contrast explains how the administrative ordering sought by the signatories could coexist with increasing insecurity for people whose family and social ties crossed the new boundary. [18] [21] Przemyśl makes these changes tangible. German forces had occupied the city before the revised partition placed its principal part under Soviet control. Yad Vashem’s account records German killings of Jews and the burning of synagogues, followed under Soviet authority by the dissolution of Jewish political parties and the subordination of communal institutions to municipal control. Some synagogues continued religious and relief work. Relief at the departure of perpetrators of immediate violence could therefore coexist with fear of the new authorities and the loss of independent organisation. Neither response can be converted into a general verdict on how all Jews, Poles or Ukrainians experienced the change. [34] The treaty distributed control without creating the complete administrative machinery through which either occupier would govern. Germany’s annexation measures and the General Government belonged to the following month; the Soviet incorporation measures followed on **1–2 November**. Keeping those steps separate explains what the September agreement achieved: it reduced conflict between the invaders over their respective territorial claims, leaving each substantial room to impose its own institutions. The [study of 26 October](/articles/german-occupation-administration-1939-10-26) examines the resulting German arrangements and the parallel Soviet process. [1] [35]

A settlement Poland refused

Friendship in the treaty’s title denoted a practical relationship built around territorial allocation, political repression, migration and economic exchange. These commitments could operate while the governments retained incompatible longer ambitions. Their joint peace declaration sought a further result: acceptance by Britain and France of the situation produced through conquest. The treaty’s durability therefore depended both on cooperation between the occupiers and on decisions beyond their control, including continued Allied belligerency and the survival of Polish diplomatic opposition. [25] [18] Poland’s rejection left the settlement’s claim to finality unresolved. Berlin and Moscow could regulate withdrawals, administer territory and control crossings, but they could not provide Polish consent to those arrangements. The government reconstituted in France and its continuing recognition sustained that objection internationally. Within the occupied country, however, the immediate balance of power enabled officials to impose demands concerning residence, property and work. The following October chapter examines how the territorial settlement acquired these institutions of daily rule. [2] [24]
author: R.G. Cruise
location: Moscow, occupied Poland and the European capitals
summary: The revised frontier was only part of the bargain. Secret protocols, resource agreements and a peace initiative reveal how Germany and the Soviet Union sought to consolidate their conquests—and how Poland refused to accept its disappearance.

sourceMethod: The study checks the supplied dossier against published treaty texts, German diplomatic records, contemporary American cables, parliamentary proceedings, museum research and peer-reviewed scholarship. Official justifications, diplomatic predictions and retrospective testimony are identified as such. The French premier’s October broadcast is cited through the British parliamentary record. Transcriptions were consulted rather than original manuscript images. Selected migration provisions are distinguished from subsequent deportations; signature, ratification, demarcation and annexation are dated separately. Numbered links lead to the records below, with a return link to each source’s first use.
